https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/03/elha.text: Menü Kereső Elhagyta Oroszországot a háborúellenes Borisz Nagyezsgyin Külföld Vida Benjámin Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Egy időre elhagyta Oroszországot a háborúellenes Borisz Nagyezsgyin, akit nemrég külföldi ügynöknek minősített az orosz igazságügyi minisztérium , hogy ne indulhasson a szeptemberi parlamenti választáson – írta a Reuters . „Sziasztok! Van egy jó hírem: élek és szabad vagyok. Sajnos jelenleg nem Oroszországban tartózkodom” – mondta Nagyezsgyin a Telegramon közzétett videójában, amit a párizsi Eiffel-torony előtt vett fel. Hozzátette, hogy először rendezni szeretné gondolatait, és eldönteni, hogyan tovább. A terveiről majd később számol be. A 63 éves Nagyezsgyin, aki korábban liberális parlamenti képviselő is volt, régóta nyílt bírálója Oroszország ukrajnai háborújának. Más ellenzéki politikusokhoz hasonlóan ő is az orosz politikai rendszer szigorú szabályaihoz igazodva próbálta folytatni a közéleti szerepvállalását. Távozásával azonban újabb ellenzéki hang tűnt el Oroszországból. Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök legtöbb ismert bírálója manapság vagy börtönben van, vagy külföldi száműzetésben él. Nagyezsgyint azután nyilvánították külföldi ügynöknek, hogy júniusban beadta a szeptemberi parlamenti választáson való induláshoz szükséges dokumentumokat. Az orosz törvények értelmében külföldi ügynökök nem indulhatnak választásokon. Az igazságügyi minisztérium szerint Nagyezsgyin részt vett más külföldi ügynökök és nemkívánatos szervezetek által készített anyagok létrehozásában és terjesztésében, hamis információkat terjesztett az orosz hatóságok döntéseiről és Oroszország választási rendszeréről, valamint illegális tüntetéseken és sztrájkokon való részvételre buzdított. Később a rendőrség is kihallgatta, majd egy bíróság pénzbírságot szabott ki rá, mert szélsőséges jelképeket jelenített meg a közösségi médiában. Nagyezsgyin nevetségesnek nevezte a vádat, és akkor azt mondta, hogy a hatóságok el akarják hallgattatni, kiszorítják a politikából, és megnehezítik az életét. Nagyezsgyint 2024-ben az orosz elnökválasztásból is kizárták , akkor arra hivatkoztak a hatóságok, hogy érvénytelenek voltak az indulását támogató aláírások. Vlagyimir Putyin végül 87 százalékos eredménnyel nyerte meg az elnökválasztást. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Pedro Sánchez speaking in Ceuta, Spain, last week. ‘He called out the ‘prejudice, misinformation and attacks’ of many of his [EU] peers.’ Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/Reuters View image in fullscreen Pedro Sánchez speaking in Ceuta, Spain, last week. ‘He called out the ‘prejudice, misinformation and attacks’ of many of his [EU] peers.’ Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/Reuters Spain Spain’s Pedro Sánchez is a progressive outlier in Europe – and over Ceuta, he is being made to pay for it Eoghan Gilmartin The Spanish PM has been one of few European leaders to stand up to Trump. He now faces coercive diplomacy and an emboldened far right at home Thu 6 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Share T he dramatic footage last Thursday of thousands of migrants entering Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta generated an online frenzy among the far right. And the alarmist rhetoric was also evident in the European mainstream, as EU leaders wasted little time attributing the chaotic scenes to Spain’s liberal immigration policies. In a letter organised by Italy and Denmark, and signed by 22 EU heads of government, they appeared to blame the crisis on Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s recent programme to regularise undocumented migrants, which received more than a million applications . They argued that Europe must “[address] all policies that can serve as pull factors”. This reaction displayed a striking lack of solidarity with a fellow EU member state. In an angry response, Sánchez called out the “prejudice, misinformation and attacks” of many of his peers. Yet his defiance, as well as the subsequent attempts by Brussels to display a united front , could not dispel the image of his government’s isolation during an acute emergency on its southern border. The Spanish prime minister might have taken a more prominent role on the world stage over the last year, above all through his opposition to the US war on Iran , but the Ceuta crisis also points to the narrowing margins for his brand of progressive foreign policy. In reality, Sánchez’s pursuit of accommodation with Morocco’s repressive monarchy – particularly over its occupation of the disputed territory of Western Sahara – stands at odds with his otherwise principled agenda on Palestine, Ukraine and Iran. And Ceuta is at the heart of this concession on values. Though unprecedented in scale, this is not the first time such an incident has taken place on the highly militarised border separating Morocco from the exclave. The EU’s response to the last mass incursion in 2021 was notably different. Then, after 10,000 mostly Moroccan citizens arrived in a 48-hour period, the European parliament closed ranks, adopting a resolution that accused Morocco of endangering their lives so as to exert “political pressure against Spain”. There seems little doubt that last week’s events, constituting a humanitarian tragedy in which at least 141 people died , also bore the hallmarks of such coercive diplomacy. Reports that Moroccan border guards offered little resistance during the influx, and even encouraged migrants to cross, followed a familiar playbook. Over the last decade, the Moroccan government has periodically relaxed border enforcement during moments of diplomatic tension with Spain , provoking mass crossings as a means of exerting pressure. View image in fullscreen Police officers guard a group of migrants at El Trampolin beach in Ceuta, Spain on 4 August 2026. Photograph: Reduan/EPA Five years ago, Europe recognised that dynamic. This time, much of the political debate has instead focused on point-scoring against Spain’s centre-left administration. For Sánchez, this was a sharp reminder that the rightward shift in the EU has left him operating as a progressive outlier. Italy’s Giorgia Meloni is not the only leader to treat the crisis as an opportunity to press for a harder line on migration . Those fomenting internal EU divisions simply underscored Europe’s weakness as a geopolitical actor: when faced with an apparent hybrid attack against a member state, it was unable to coordinate a collective response. The fact that Sánchez’s government was caught off guard also suggests a degree of complacency over the potential consequences of its refusal to allow the US access to its airbases during the Iran war. In the months prior to the border surge, prominent Republicans had already urged the Trump administration to retaliate by backing Morocco’s territorial claims to Ceuta, and Spain’s other north African exclave, Melilla. The combination of this sharp decline in US-Spanish relations, and Morocco’s increasing importance as a regional partner for the Trump White House , may have emboldened the country’s regime to once again target the border. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion The right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen again | Ruben Andersson Read more Alongside Trump’s threats to cut off trade with Spain, his administration has also intervened more directly in Spanish domestic politics in recent months. Just weeks after Sánchez made his stand on Iran, the US Department of Homeland Security supplied messages from a cloned phone to Spanish corruption investigators that appeared to suggest former Socialist prime minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero may have lobbied for a pandemic-era loan for a Spanish airline with links to Venezuela. Few in Madrid doubt the political motivation for this intelligence transfer, and the ensuing political storm killed most of Sánchez’s momentum from his popular anti-war stance – as Zapatero, a key ally, was put under formal investigation. The coordinated pile-on from Trump and the wider Maga universe over the Ceuta crisis also raises the prospect of further efforts from Washington to target Sánchez politically, ahead of next year’s Spanish general election. Any such efforts would find a willing domestic partner in the Vox party, which has stood apart from much of Europe’s populist right by remaining uncritically aligned with Trump, even during the Iran war. Vox is Spain’s fastest-growing party since the 2023 general election, is polling in the high teens , and will play a pivotal role in any future rightwing alternative to Sánchez’s government. With that threat rumbling in the background, the Spanish PM must also navigate relations with Morocco in the wake of its latest act of coercion. Rather than publicly confronting Rabat, Sánchez has prioritised restoring cooperation and quickly containing the crisis, with the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 arrivals returned to Morocco within 24 hours. Yet this pragmatism carries obvious risks. Spain’s last major confrontation with Morocco in 2021-22 ended in a historic concession, as Sánchez abandoned decades of Spanish neutrality on Western Sahara to back Morocco’s plan to incorporate the former Spanish colony as an autonomous region within the Moroccan state. Last week’s events suggest this strategy of accommodation has failed to deliver the long-term stability in relations which Madrid sought. Sánchez’s leftwing coalition partner, Sumar, is now demanding a tougher line – including that Spain refuses to co-host the 2030 World Cup with Morocco . Morocco’s exact motives for acting now remain open to debate. The most plausible explanation lies in Sánchez’s visit to Algiers 10 days earlier to seal Spain’s rapprochement with its key gas supplier, Algeria, which is also Morocco’s chief rival over Western Sahara. The Ceuta crisis was probably the Moroccan regime’s reminder that any attempts by Madrid to rebalance its north African policies remain subject to its influence over migration flows. It also likely reflects Morocco’s longer-term ambition to advance its claims on Ceuta and Melilla, at a time when control of maritime checkpoints like the strait of Gibraltar have acquired renewed geopolitical importance. At the height of the crisis, Spain’s combative transport minister, Óscar Puente, posted on social media that he wanted “Spain to be a sovereign nation in an interconnected world, not a subsidiary of Trump or Netanyahu”. With much of Europe’s political class lying supine before Trump, Sánchez has been the most outspoken western leader willing to challenge Washington, not just on Iran, but also in rejecting the 5% defence spending target , pushing the EU to end its association agreement with Israel , and forging closer ties with China and nations of the global south . This is not an index of Sánchez’s radicalism so much as his wager that Spain has more to gain from adapting to the new geography of global economic power than it does from clinging to the old Atlantic order. Ceuta, however, is a reminder that such a wager is fraught with danger. https://www.thejc.com/opinion/god-save-n.text: Is New York still for Jews? Since October 7 and the rise of Mamdani and the “Habibi City” movement, as New York Magazine put it in their viral issue this week, it seems like the quick answer is no. And indeed, Jews are leaving New York. Though there are no official stats (it is still not common practice in the US to keep lists of Jews), what we do know is that the number of Florida’s new residents from New York grew by over 500,000 in the last 12 months, according to the US census. It’s not an exodus, but it’s happening. And can you blame people for wanting to move to greener pastures (or humid marshlands) to live among their own and significantly lower their tax payments? An American friend of mine, whom I met in London, where we both live, texted me the following sentence from said promised swampland just last week: “Miami is the most Jewish city and oasis with zero Jew hate… It has been an antidote to the nonstop hate we have in the UK.” Yes, he actually texted me that. Even if Jews aren’t moving, they are seriously thinking about it – at least the non-vehemently antizionist majority. This means that the place they helped make so great, New York, is seeming to many like it is no longer for them. But I, a European Jew living in London, am writing to tell you that this is not true. It is simply not what I saw when I was there recently. I saw a city brimming with loud, confident and overt Jewish life. A (large) temple on every other block with minimal security (in comparison to London’s fortress-synagogues), face after face on the street that looked like my cousins, and shops with “Happy Passover” signs in the windows. In London, shop windows I have seen display posters in the shape of Israel, coloured entirely red, with bold writing in Arabic scrawled across them. I don’t mean to downplay the problems for Jews in New York; they are there. Antisemitism is no longer taboo: intimidation masquerading as “protests”, the degradation of education at all levels… the list goes on. I don’t need to tell you that these political problems are not easily solved. Even if every Jew in New York voted against the Democratic Socialists of America (and it is difficult to imagine all Jews agreeing on anything), the dial would not move much. Jews are, despite often having larger-than-life personalities, still a minority, even in Jew York. When I hear about antisemitism taking hold in New York, I have two reactions. First, I share the sense of betrayal with my fellow Jews over there. Even three years after October 7, I still feel that jab when I see a “Zionism = Nazism” banner on the Instagram story of a long-lost acquaintance from art school who moved to New York to pursue their dream of being free to attend Pride-themed, pro-Palestine block parties in Brooklyn. Don’t they know they are stomping to the beat of a Troye Sivan hit – yes, Jewish Troye Sivan – on hallowed Jewish ground? The second reaction is letting out a long, audible sigh: are there really no new ideas? Is the biggest tragedy of our times that, politically, humanity has lost the ability to innovate? Can we please just move on from the Jews? In Europe this is clear. We have been almost completely erased after many successful attempts to eradicate us, both literally and culturally. You will only find our impact on European civilisation if you know where to look. But in New York it is not like that. The Jewishness is unavoidable. It’s everywhere you look. I couldn’t take this visibility for granted when I was there. I was so moved. I was trotting merrily down Lexington on my way to try the matzo ball soup at Pastrami Queen. I was staying near Yorkville with an old friend who currently lives there. After she had gone to the office, I had spent almost an hour deciding which Jewish deli would be on my daily lunchtime pilgrimage, overwhelmed by the sheer amount of choice. As I crossed the street to get some coffee from a place that looked vaguely European (the only bad thing about New York is the coffee), a glint of sun blinded me momentarily. It had reflected into my eyes from a row of parked Hatzolah ambulances on the other side of the road. They were just there, out in the open, shimmering on a glorious spring day. The British equivalent of these had been incinerated just weeks prior, in an act of violent antisemitic intimidation. I was overcome with a feeling of pride. The next time I was struck by this feeling, I was at the museums. At the Frick Collection, it felt like Europe on steroids – in a good way. Almost exact replicas, room by room, of the galleries I have visited all over my own continent, but bigger, better and shinier. I noted the many Jewish names on the walls, of course. I was feeling invigorated, starting to catch New York’s magnetic optimism by that point. An optimism which is also very Jewish, in its unwavering determination to believe in miracles. It is even in the very shape of the city, which literally reaches for the sky. I was filled with a sense of awe as I headed to my next stop, the park in full cherry blossom bloom to my left. By the time I crossed into the Beaux-Arts foyer of the Neue Galerie, my guard was completely down. Making my way up the curve of the staircase, again, I felt I was seeing a buffed reflection of my own experience. From my mother’s side, my family hails from this lost world of Austro-Hungarian glamour recreated so accurately at the Neue Galerie. My own grandmother was a chic woman of mysterious allure who, until the end of her days, was haunted by the horrors of the Holocaust and the later Soviet invasion of Budapest. I stopped in front of Berlin Street Scene by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner: aliens in fur-lined coats and protruding hats, swishing elegantly by on a winter eve. I read the placard. I hadn’t known it had been restituted. What a joy! This made me think of another work by Kirchner in my hometown, in Madrid: Fränzi in Front of a Carved Chair at the Thyssen-Bornemisza. Why is the provenance of that painting, especially around the 1930s and 1940s, not on the wall? Could the answer have something to do with what happens when you type into Google search “Nazi connection” after the Thyssen-Bornemisza family name? I made my way through the somehow familiar rooms. Turning a corner, she was suddenly there. Adele Bloch-Bauer in Gustav Klimt’s hand. Having only seen reproductions before, I was stunned to see her Jewish beauty in the flesh. So exquisite. Of course, she too was restituted by the force of American litigation and diplomacy. A rescued Jewish treasure, looking back at me in New York. “Could all of this be partly mine?” I thought. “Could a part of me belong to the greatest city in the world?” I shed a tear. Could this have been what Vienna felt like to Jews before the 1930s, or Alexandria before 414, or Toledo before 1492? Following this arc of history, it is easy to believe that Jewish existence in the diaspora always ends in despair. But in New York, most days, Jewish life outweighs the pain. I saw a queue of tourists from all over the world winding around the block for pastrami and corned beef sandwiches at Katz’s, Trader Joe’s own version of Bamba readily available on the shelves, and half of the Upper West Side gone for Passover. The fact that the world’s most consequential city is so Jewish is a lucky historical accident – a miracle – one that I know you won’t let go without a (figurative) fight. There is too much at stake for global Jewry if we don’t remind people that we, just like everyone else, have a right to be in the middle of it all. Working at the Jewish Chronicle, the world’s oldest Jewish newspaper still in print, I have a front-row seat to ever-increasing Jew-hatred in the UK, and the wider region. I recently interviewed the star of The Producers here in London, Andy Nyman, and in our conversation he admitted that he wasn’t sure non-Jewish audiences understood just how “Jewish the show is… I think they think it’s just ‘New York-y’.” And although this may be somewhat sad, it is also not. Because this is how synonymous the two words are. New York is the capital of world Jewry (sorry, Tel Aviv, but your day will come). As Jews, we are alert to political decay because it so easily turns against us. Right now, this decay is a global phenomenon. And, of course, in New York and in America, it is visible too. But the difference between America and the rest of the world is that the decay has not yet turned into rot. And, in my opinion, it is unlikely to. New York is very far from Fidel’s Havana or, from my vantage point, Sadiq Khan’s London. It is too American, too capitalist and too free for that to happen. In America, you still have freedom of speech, a highly competent democracy, an elastic economy, unparalleled positivity and people who care. And a constitution into which Jews are almost enshrined, admired by the Founding Fathers as the original Israelites. These are things we are leaving behind in Europe, or never really had. In America, the state religion is freedom, and New York is the apple of the eye of everyone who values it. So, I’m writing to you from London to say this: to my fellow Jews of the far East (Coast), we are with you. What you and your forebears built, not only for yourselves but for all of us, is far too precious to surrender. Michelle Wolodarsky is the JC's Social Media Editor

https://www.dw.com/en/uk-announces-trade.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5M7qN Foreign Secrety Ed Miliband announced the measures in the House of Commons [File: July 29, 2026] Image: Leon Neal/PA Images/picture alliance Advertisement The United Kingdom on Tuesday announced trade restrictions on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank . The center-left Labour Party government has previously sanctioned some Israeli settlers and illegal outposts over violence against Palestinians and illegal development in the West Bank. The announcement came as the foreign ministers of 11 other governments announced they too would be slapping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements. Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden also plan to limit trade with the settlements, according to a joint statement. Meanwhile, an EU Foreign Affairs spokesperson said the bloc "adopted three packages of sanctions against extreme settlers and their entities." What did Miliband say? "I can announce today that we will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced in the House of Commons. "We will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion," Miliband said. The foreign secretary said those financing or facilitating illegal settlement would "face the full force of UK sanctions." Before announcing the sanctions, Miliband said that "settler terrorism was rampant" and referenced various instances of violence in the West Bank. Miliband told MPs a "new approach" was necessary because plans for development in the West Bank would render a two-state solution "unviable" as it would be "cutting through the heart of Palestine." Miliband accused the Israeli government of turning a "blind eye" to what he called "ethnic cleansing" by settlers in the West Bank. Why is the UK restricting trade The measures appear to be setting the tone for relations between Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Israel. According to a Downing Street readout of a phone call between the British leader and US President Donald Trump on the phone on Monday, Burnham laid out "the UK's commitment to working towards peace and security in the region," and stressed the importance of a two-state solution in Israel and the Palestinian territories . The United Kingdom recognized Palestinian statehood last year in an attempt to revive efforts to achieve a two-state solution. It also comes Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government forges ahead with settlement construction in the West Bank , raising fears among some Western governments that it threatens any possible two-state solution. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law. The measures also come amd flaring tensions in the West Bank that have involved violent attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers. The UK has previously condemned the violence while calling for civilians to be protected and for those responsible to be held accountable. Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Palestinian Authority welcomed the announcement of sanctions, calling the measures "an important step" to accountability. "This as an important practical step toward holding the settlement system accountable and demonstrating non-recognition of the unlawful situation created by the occupation," Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas's office said in a statement. Israel orders closure of UK consulate in Jerusalem Ahead of the announcement, Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar already indicated that Israel would respond. "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain," Saar warned. Saar ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem once the measures became known. "The accusations made today by the foreign secretary in the British Parliament were outrageous lies," Saar said in response to Miliband accusing Israeli settlers of ethnic cleansing in the occupied Palestinian territory. Israel's hard-line public security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly recognize the Falkland Islands as "Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently steal from the Argentine people." [Photo/Xinhua] Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Tuesday that the European Union (EU) should pursue "friendly competition" with China rather than treat the country as an enemy and put up barriers. Fico made the remarks after talks in Bratislava with European Council President Antonio Costa, who began his annual tour of EU capitals in Slovakia. Their discussions covered the EU's next long-term budget, competitiveness, energy prices and enlargement. Fico said Slovakia was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally, arguing that greater competitiveness should not mean imposing new tariffs or barriers, but rather striving to do better and outperform others. "I have a different view about relations between the EU and China. I don't think we should fight China by putting up barriers and treating it as an enemy," Fico said. "China is a country with which we should compete in a friendly spirit and strive to do better." On the EU's next long-term budget, Fico said Slovakia supported maintaining a strong cohesion policy to reduce regional disparities across the bloc. "We're even saying that some extra funding should be found for countries in the eastern part of the EU, which, for example, share borders with Ukraine," he said, adding that a strong agricultural policy is another key Slovak priority. The two leaders also discussed EU enlargement. Fico reiterated Slovakia's support for countries seeking membership, but said all applicants must meet the required criteria. "That means no exceptions and no shortcuts. And that also applies to Ukraine," he stressed. Fico said Ukraine should not be allowed to overtake countries such as Montenegro, Albania or Serbia in the accession process, arguing that they had been preparing for EU membership for much longer. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: The aftermath of a Russian drone strike on one of two petrol stations targeted on Friday. Photograph: Alina Smutko/Reuters View image in fullscreen The aftermath of a Russian drone strike on one of two petrol stations targeted on Friday. Photograph: Alina Smutko/Reuters Ukraine Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones Three facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensity Europe live – latest updates Amy Hawkins in Kyiv Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.01 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 10.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity. At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday, the first of its kind in the capital. At the Ukrnafta petrol station in the Pochaina neighbourhood in northern Kyiv , bystanders said three people had been injured in Friday’s blast – the manager of a nearby car wash, his wife and the driver of a passing car. The blown-out vehicle was stranded by the side of the road, its windows shattered and seats spattered in blood. Witnesses said they had heard two explosions, and local authorities later said Russia had carried out a double-tap attack on the facility. View image in fullscreen Pochaina petrol station. All three strikes targeted sites operated by Ukrnafta Photograph: Amy Hawkins “This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster,” said Anastasiia Demchenko, 30, who works at a delivery company opposite the petrol station. “It feels like life is on the edge.” All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company. Sergiy Fedorenko, the acting head of Naftogaz, Ukrnafta’s parent company, said: “There is, and can be, no military objective behind such attacks. This is terror directed at the civilian population, at peaceful people.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Kyiv suffers hours of daytime air raids as Russia deploys new jet-powered drones Read more A list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. The three struck so far were on the list. At the other station hit on Friday, in Desnianskyi district, one of the most densely populated parts of the capital, the manager of a nearby car wash said it had been a miracle that no one had died in the blast. Fedir Lesovin said the air-raid siren had given the petrol station workers time to run to a nearby shelter, and that a customer waiting outside his business saw the incoming drone and also ran to safety. View image in fullscreen Desnianskyi district petrol station was also hit, in one of the most densely populated areas of Kyiv. Photograph: Amy Hawkins Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian petrol stations in recent months. Facilities in the east and south of the country have been repeatedly targeted, but this week’s attacks mark the first time that strikes against a vital part of daily life have been brought to the capital. Ukraine has also targeted Russian oil infrastructure. Its special forces said this week that they had struck facilities at the Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala. Kyiv has been pounded by daily drone and missile strikes since late August, at a time when Ukraine is running low on Patriot interceptors . A brief reprieve for the visit of the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff over the weekend ended on Monday. The petrol station attacks happened as Volodymyr Zelenskyy was on an overseas trip intended to drum up international support and aid before what is expected to be a difficult winter. On Thursday the Ukrainian president met Canada’s prime minister , Mark Carney, who offered support to help boost Ukraine’s drone stocks. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6z9.text: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Aliko Dangote made his fortune from cement in Nigeria By Ondiro Oganga Published 4 hours ago Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has announced that he is helping to fund a new $660m (Â£500m) fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres. It is expected to begin operations within 18 months. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline would reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one. The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol. Speaking at the ground-breaking ceremony, Dangote, Africa's richest man, said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient. Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction. Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues. The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa. Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day. The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (Â£1.2bn). In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu. Photograph: Sussex police Brighton Three sisters who drowned in Brighton took their own lives, inquest finds Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters from London visited late mother’s former home shortly before their deaths in May Esther Addley Thu 8 Oct 2026 08.20 EDT First published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three sisters who drowned in the sea in Brighton collectively decided to end their own lives, a coroner has ruled. The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, all from London , were recovered from the sea off Brighton in the early hours of 13 May. An inquest into their deaths heard on Thursday that in the days before they died, the three women made a trip together to Birmingham to visit the former home of their mother, who died by drowning in 2010. The inquest at Woodvale coroner’s court in Brighton heard that the sisters travelled by taxi to Birmingham on 11 May and were dropped off at 11.36pm at Linton Walk. The address is close to Brookvale Park Lake, where their mother, Janice Adetoro, died. They were picked up to return to the flat they lived in together in Greenford, west London, at 1.28am on 12 May. DCI Mark Cullimore, of Sussex police, told the hearing there was no CCTV to show what the women did in the time they were in Birmingham. On the evening of 12 May, they took a pre-booked taxi to Brighton and arrived near the seafront at 10.21pm. They are thought to have last been seen alive on CCTV from the beach at 2.42am on 13 May. The bodies of Jane Adetoro and Christina Walters were located by a RNLI lifeboat crew; Rebecca Walters’ body was recovered from the shoreline on Brighton beach. The senior coroner Penelope Schofield told the court on Thursday: “In hours of darkness, they entered the sea at Brighton, they could not swim and sea conditions were adverse.” A postmortem found all three women had drowned. There was no evidence of any drugs or alcohol in their bodies and no evidence to suggest they had been subjected to violence. The coroner concluded that the medical cause of death for all three women was drowning and that they had died by suicide. Schofield told the court: “These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private. We don’t know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton. It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known.” The inquest heard that Christina Walters had suffered from anxiety and depression since her mother’s death, but no such issues were recorded for her sister Rebecca. Adetoro was not registered with a doctor. The women’s father, Joseph Jacobson, who attended the hearing by video link, said in a written statement: “There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. To lose all three of my precious daughters, Jane, Christina and Rebecca, is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined.” He said he could not understand why their lives had ended so suddenly, adding: “You were my daughters, you will always be my daughters and I will love you for the rest of my life. May your beautiful souls rest in perfect peace.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org . In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Bernard Walsh/Netflix Â© 2025 | BERNARD WALSH/NETFLIX Netflix has been on a final season kick, and it seems one of its biggest shows might soon be joining the list of hit shows ending with a final season in 2027.Â On Wednesday, September 30, Netflix announced that production had finally wrapped on Wednesday season 3 , sharing a new behind-the-scenes photo of Jenna Ortega in character to commemorate the moment. The announcement kept things rather simple and was used to literally just inform fans that production had ended with no further details provided about the third season, such as a release window, but there was one aspect of the release that caught the eyes of some fans.Â When announcing the end of production, Netflix touted that âthe coffin is closed,â which some began to read into as a hint that the framing was a subtle clue that Netflix was about to close the door on Wednesday with its third season serving as its final season. At first, it seemed like fans were reading too much into the wording, but then came a pair of posts from Ortegaâs stunt double Jenny Ayumi, which seem to hint this really is the end for Wednesday.Â Shortly after Netflix announced that production had ended on season 3, Ayumi took to social media to commemorate the end of production in a manner that certainly suggests Wednesday season 3 will be the showâs last.Â âEnd of an era. A 5-year chapter finally comes to a close,â Ayumi wrote on the first post shared to her Instagram Stories ( h/t Collider ). She then followed that story up with a throwback to the first season which she captioned, âA little throwback to where it all began 5 years ago in Romania.âÂ Interestingly, shortly after posting the two stories, Ayumi deleted the first of the two, which has only further fueled speculation that Wednesday season 3 will be the showâs final season. Many fans have seen the removal of the first message as a case of Ayumi backtracking after sharing information that wasnât yet meant to be public. Weâve seen this happen many times over the years in which a member of a production team, be it someone on the cast or crew, posts an update that has not yet been known and then quickly deletes the post, realizing they shared something that was not yet announced.Â Unfortunately, the internet is forever, and fans are always quick to screenshot and screenrecord posts and then circulate them on social media even after their removal. This was the case earlier this week when a writersâ assistant accidentally confirmed the Bridgerton season lead .Â Should Wednesday indeed come to an end with season 3, itâll join a growing list of Netflix Originals to end with a final season in 2027, including hits such as The Night Agent and The Lincoln Lawyer. But hey, at least they're getting final seasons! Other Netflix shows have not been as lucky, and a three-season run for Wednesday seems perfect given that the character's time at Nevermore Academy is coming to an end.
